values.dcuBody: The season plan is filled from Cycling Denmark's recommendations for the rider's age class, and the strength programmes for U17, U19 and U23 are ready. The coach can deviate, and the deviation is always visible. The AI can propose next week; the coach decides.
values.dataBody: The rider decides what parents see. Everything can be exported as a spreadsheet and JSON in one click and deleted completely.
values.securityBody: Teams are separated in the database, and so are riders: a teammate never sees your check-ins. Passkeys, two-factor sign-in and a log that cannot be edited.

ways.label: Two ways to use Kadence
ways.teamBody: The coach lays sessions in the riders' calendars, sees the team's week and who is worth a talk. The riders ride, and parents follow what the rider shares. The club applies, and we set the team up.
ways.aloneBody: You plan your own week and season, add your rides and check in, without being on a team. If you are U17, U19 or U23, DCU's numbers stand beside yours; if you are an adult, you set your own hours. Join a team later and your training comes with you.
ways.aloneAge: From 15 you create your own account. For a younger rider, a parent creates it and follows the child's training.

dataExport.title: Data and export
dataExport.subtitle: Take a complete copy of everything this workspace holds.
dataExport.xlsxBody: One file with a tab per kind of data: riders, sessions, activities, check-ins, calendar, comments, season plans, templates and history. For yourselves, or for anyone who needs to look without knowing Kadence.
dataExport.jsonBody: The same data as JSON, with every id kept. It is the file that lets you move to something other than Kadence without losing the links between sessions, activities and comments.
dataExport.auditNote: The audit trail in the spreadsheet is the newest {rows, number} rows. The whole trail is in the JSON file.
dataExport.filesBody: The original file from every ride, in one zip with a folder per rider. These are the files from the watch, the bike computer or Rulle, as they came in.
dataExport.limitedExport: The export has been downloaded three times in this workspace in the last hour. You can download it again in {minutes} min.

dataExport.notBackupBody: An export can be read but not restored, and it is only as fresh as the day you downloaded it. The night's encrypted dump is what saves you when the database is gone.
dataExport.privacy: The export holds what you may see in the workspace and its history: a coach gets the whole team, a rider their own data. Passwords, passkeys, device tokens and the workspace's model key never go in it. That you downloaded the file is written to the audit trail.

ai.title: AI
ai.subtitle: Which engine answers, and what it is allowed to do.
ai.providerHint: The installation sets a model in the environment, and each workspace can choose its own instead.

model.title: Your own language model
model.subtitle: This workspace can run on a different model than the installation set up. Choose nothing and you inherit the installation's.
model.providerHelp: The Ollama address is set by the installation. That is deliberate: a workspace that could point at an address of its own would make the server fetch from anywhere.
model.modelHelpMistral: Leave the field empty to use {placeholder}.
model.modelHelpOllama: The name must match a model you have pulled with “ollama pull”. Test the connection above and it will list the ones you have.
model.keyHelp: Leave the field empty to use the installation's key. The key is encrypted before it is stored and cannot be read back.
model.keyStoredHelp: This workspace has its own key. Type a new one to replace it, or remove it to fall back on the installation's.
model.saveFailed: Could not be saved. Try again.
model.notAllowed: Only owners and administrators can change the workspace's model.
model.planExpired: The workspace is read only now, so the setting was not saved.

ai.setupIntro: Kadence is a chat and cannot answer without a model. Set one up:
ai.setupOutro: Then start Kadence again. Without a model the writing field says so, and settings, roles and tasks can still be edited.
ai.limitsHint: A model call costs money on a hosted installation and minutes on a local one. The numbers are generous for a person and mean for a script.
ai.perMonthOwnKey: This workspace uses its own key and pays for itself, so the budget does not apply.
ai.messageLength: Characters in a message, at most
ai.principleDecides: The AI answers, the person decides. The model writes an answer; it never sends anything out of the house, never deletes anything and changes nothing unless you do.
ai.principleUndo: Every conversation is your own. You can delete it, and you can take it out.
ai.principleData: What you write, and what your documents contain, is sent to the model as data, never as instructions. The system prompt and the roles live on the server, where the administrator sets them.
ai.principleSovereign: The model can be swapped, including for a local one. Who can see what is listed in docs/subprocessors.md.
ai.testPatience: A local model may have to be read off disk first. That can take up to a minute the first time.
ai.failAuth: The key was rejected. Check the workspace's own key below, or the installation's MISTRAL_API_KEY.
ai.failUnreachable: Nothing is listening at that address. Is Ollama running? Check OLLAMA_BASE_URL.
ai.failConfig: The model is set up wrong. Correct the model name below, or ask the installation's owner to correct it.
ai.failGeneric: The call failed. The details are below and in the server log.
ai.failRateLimited: Mistral has said stop for now. The key works, but the account's ceiling is reached or the model is busy. Try again in a little while. If it happens often, a paid plan at Mistral can help.
ai.failWhereToLook: The details are in the server log.
ai.testNotAllowed: Only the owner or an administrator can test the connection.
ai.withoutBody: Kadence is built around the conversation: without a model you can still see your conversations, take them out and edit the workspace's roles and tasks, but the writing field says so plainly, and nothing breaks.
ai.perInstallation: Calls across the installation per day
ai.failBudget: The workspace's AI budget for the month is spent, so the AI rests until next month. The installation's owner can give it more.
ai.failPlanExpired: The workspace is read only now, so the AI does not answer. See Settings → Subscription.
ai.failCeiling: Kadence's own ceiling on AI calls was reached, not the provider's. The ceilings are under “Ceiling on AI calls” below; the installation's own is set with AI_DAILY_CALL_CAP. Try again shortly.

terms.title: Terms and privacy
terms.intro: Kadence is an open source tool for training planning for young cyclists, run by Haij. This is the agreement between you and us when you use the edition we run. If you run the code yourself, only the licence applies.

what.title: What Kadence is
what.body: A tool to plan and follow training for riders, coaches and parents: sessions in a calendar, activities from FIT files and devices, check-ins and a season plan. Recommendations and AI proposals are drafts, not answers, and replace neither a coach nor a doctor.

account.title: Accounts and access
account.body: You get in by applying or being invited. We store your name, your email and your workspace's name, and use them to sign you in and to show who you are on the team. Passwords are stored hashed, and you can add a passkey and two-factor. We sell nothing, and we do not send marketing you did not ask for.

yourData.title: Your data
yourData.body: Everything you write in Kadence belongs to you and your team, and a rider's training and check-ins belong to the rider. It can be downloaded as a spreadsheet and JSON in one click and deleted again. We do not look at it unless you ask us for help, and we never pass it on.

ai.title: AI
ai.body: With a language model set up, when a coach asks for a proposal, what it builds on — sessions, load and, if the team has turned it on, check-ins — is sent to the model provider. Who that is, is under Settings → AI and in the list of subprocessors. Without a model everything else works as before.

leaving.title: Leaving
leaving.body: You can delete your workspace immediately, without writing to anyone and without waiting. The export is one click away and readable without Kadence. We keep no copy afterwards beyond the nightly encrypted backups, which roll off after 30 days — on the server and in the EU storage they are copied to.

availability.title: Operation and guarantees
availability.body: Kadence is new, and there is no uptime guarantee. We look after your data with encrypted backups every night, but you should download an export now and then. The service is provided as is, without guarantees beyond what mandatory law requires.

license.title: Licence
license.body: The code is AGPL-3.0. You may use it, change it and run it yourself; if you change it and offer it to others over a network, your changes must be available too. What you write in the tool is not covered by the licence — that is yours.

demo.title: The demo
demo.body: A demo workspace is created without e-mail or sign-up and deleted entirely after 24 hours, account included. Do not put real personal data in it. We keep only the technical log data needed to keep the demo running.

contact.title: Contact
contact.body: Write to martin@vintherconsulting.dk. If you have found a security problem, SECURITY.md in the repository says how to report it; use that rather than an ordinary email.

roles.title: Who may do what
roles.body: Coaches are the workspace's owners and admins: they plan for every rider on the team. A rider sees and writes their own data and nobody else's. A parent sees their own child's training once the rider has confirmed the link, and check-ins only if the rider shares them. The database enforces it, not just the screens.

password.title: Forgotten password
password.body: If Kadence is set up to send email, the sign-in page has a link under Forgot your password, and you can get a link by email yourself. Otherwise the way back in goes through a coach. A coach opens Settings → Workspace, presses Link for a new password by the person, and sends the link on themselves, by text message for instance. The link works once and only for the next hour; whoever uses it chooses a new password and is signed out everywhere else. The person can always see on their security page that a link was made, and by whom. A coach can make links for riders, parents and other coaches on the team, but not for the team's owner; an owner who forgot the password signs in with their passkey or gets help from whoever runs Kadence. If you have turned on two-step verification, you still need the code from your app.

words.title: Session, block, programme and season plan
words.body: A session is one training in the calendar, on the bike or in the gym. A rider's week is made of sessions. A block is several weeks of sessions from the library, applied from a Monday for one or more riders. A programme is a recipe for one strength session: exercises with drawings and doses, which becomes a session when it is put in the calendar. DCU's strength programmes are a third thing: a series of sessions with a progression, fetched into the library. The season plan is the hours month by month from October to September, with DCU's numbers beside them. An adult rider, a senior, is a motionist or a supermotionist: Kadence's own hours, about 5 or 10 a week, since DCU has none for adults. Plan the week is where the coach lays a whole week at once.

overview.title: Overview: the coach's front page
overview.body: As a coach you land on Overview. At the top it says whether next week is planned and what is in it, such as holidays, exams, camps and races, with a button to the planner for that week. Then the three riders most worth a look in the week in progress; the whole list is under the team's week in the calendar. News from the riders gathers the riders' own comments on sessions and rides and their notes from check-ins over the last 14 days, newest first. You can answer in the session's own thread. Last come the team's sessions today and the team's events this week. A rider's front page is called Today.

data.title: Your data
data.body: Everything can be downloaded as a spreadsheet and JSON under Settings → Data. The workspace can be deleted completely, audit trail included.

calendar.title: The calendar
calendar.body: The calendar shows one week at a time. On a computer the days stand side by side, on a phone one below the other, and the team's week is one card per rider. The coach can drag a session to another day; on a phone you use "Move" in the session's menu. Races, exams, school, camps, holidays and illness sit in the calendar as small labels. The colours show how it went: green is as planned, yellow is a little off, red is not done or far from the plan, and grey is not ridden yet. There is always a word beside the colour. A session can have a time and a meeting place, say "17:30 from the clubhouse". A whole week is laid in under "Plan the week": choose riders, a whole class with one tap if you like, and start from an empty week, last week, a block or a proposal from the AI. You see what the week gives against the season plan before you lay it in, and you can repeat it over several weeks or save it as a block. If one session should come back, say strength every Tuesday and Thursday, turn on "Repeat on set weekdays" when you add it; "Edit" and "Delete" can also take the rest of the series. "Copy the week before" lays each rider's own sessions from another week on the same weekdays. "Share the week" makes a text with the week's sessions, times and places for the team's chat, with nothing about the riders' wellbeing.

search.title: Search
search.body: Search finds a rider, a session from the library, a page or a section of this help. Press ⌘K on a Mac or Ctrl+K on a PC, or tap the search field at the top of the menu. On a phone it is the magnifier at the top of the screen. Type a few letters, move up and down with the arrow keys, and press Enter to open. You can type o for ø and a for å. Search only shows what you may already see: a coach finds the team's riders, a parent their own child.

sessions.title: Sessions and templates
sessions.body: A session is built in steps: warm-up, work, rest and cool-down, each with a length and a target in zones, percent of FTP or threshold heart rate, or by feel. Repeats gather steps that are ridden several times. Once the rider's thresholds are set, the targets read in watts and pulse. Strength sessions have exercises, and a programme has a progression, so sets and reps follow along from session to session. A coach can also press "Build with AI" and write the session in their own words, e.g. "5x4 min VO2max" or "strength 45 min, legs and core", or what to change in the session as it stands. The proposal is shown first, and nothing is saved until the coach saves the session. Bike sessions can be built from building blocks with one tap, say a warm-up, threshold intervals or sprints, and strength exercises are suggested as you type the name, DCU's exercises and ones without machines. Save a session as a template in the library and it can be given to one rider or the whole team at once. Several weeks of sessions can be gathered in a block and laid in from a Monday.

exercises.title: Exercises and programmes
exercises.body: Exercises and programmes with drawings live under Library → Exercises and programmes, and "Exercises and programmes" is also one of the open guides anyone can open without signing in. You choose one of Kadence's own programmes, or put together your own from the library's exercises. Download it as one file that works on a phone without the internet, or print it as a PDF from the browser. As a coach, you draw the team's own exercises with a drawing tool and build them into programmes that sit beside Kadence's own. "Put in the calendar" lays the programme in as a session, where each exercise shows its drawing. As a rider you can put a programme in your own calendar, as the coach can for the whole team.

done.title: Done and RPE
done.body: When the session is done, the rider presses "Done". The minutes are already there from the plan. Then the rider says how hard it was on a scale from 1 to 10 (RPE): 1 is very, very easy, 5 is hard, and 10 is the hardest you can. Think of the whole session. Minutes times RPE gives the session's load, even without a power meter. A wrong press can be undone.

comments.title: Comments
comments.body: Each session has one conversation. The coach and the rider write in it, and the rider's parents can read along. There are no private messages between an adult and a young rider. You can edit and delete your own comments, and a coach can remove a comment.

parents.title: Parents
parents.body: The coach adds a parent and sends a link. The parent sees nothing until the rider has confirmed the link under Settings → Profile. The rider also decides whether the parents can see the training, and whether they can see how the rider is doing. From the year the rider turns 18, the rider confirms again as an adult.

season.title: The season plan and DCU
season.body: The season runs from October to September. The plan can be filled with DCU's hours for the rider's class (U17, U19 or U23 and the year in it), month by month, with DCU's phases: break and free riding in October, distance in November and December, long base intervals in January and February, short hard intervals around March, and the racing season from April. Under "The whole team", "Create season plans for everyone without one" makes the plans for the whole team at once. The coach and the rider can change anything. When the team follows DCU's recommendations (Settings → Team), DCU's numbers and the deviation stand beside it. Wherever training is planned, the same four numbers stand: Season plan (the hours the coach has set), Scheduled (the sessions in the calendar), Ridden (what was actually ridden) and DCU (DCU's hours and the range round them). You see them for the week in the calendar, for each rider in the team's week, and month by month on the season page. Only hours on the bike count. Kadence's seven zones are Kadence's own; DCU's heart-rate bands are shown beside them for comparison.

load.title: Load: fitness, fatigue and freshness
load.body: Every session gets a load. With a power meter it is worked out from power, otherwise from heart rate, and otherwise from how hard the session felt (RPE from 1 to 10) times the minutes. The last works for every session, strength too. An hour at threshold counts 100, and an easy hour at RPE 3 about 17. Fitness is what the last six weeks have built. Fatigue is what the last week has cost. Freshness is fitness minus fatigue: above zero you are rested, below zero tired, and a little below zero is normal in the middle of a training week.

warnings.title: Points of attention
warnings.body: Kadence shows the coach when a week goes past the limits, and the coach decides what happens. The points of attention are under Calendar → The whole team: as badges beside each rider and as a list under the week, where "See the week" opens the rider's week. Overview shows the three riders most worth a look, with the way to the whole list. The points are: hours on the bike above or below DCU's range for the week (October is DCU's break and has no range), more than 15 % more hours than the last weeks, a ride longer than DCU's limit (U17 at most 4 hours or 120 km, U19 at most 5 hours or 150 km), strength sessions less than 48 hours apart, sessions far from the plan, much time in the middle zone when the team uses "Low intensity first", too little sleep, pain on ATK's pain ladder, and check-ins in the yellow or red zone. Each point has a word for how much it matters: "Important now", "Worth a look" or "Good to know". Once you have talked a point through, you can mark it resolved.

checkin.title: Check-in and wellbeing zones
checkin.body: Every morning the rider answers on sleep, energy and pain, and under "More" on how well they slept, mood, fresh legs, calm and whether they are ill. When the rider answers only the first three, the rest stay as at the last check-in. The answers give a zone for the day: green, yellow or red. Kadence looks at the pattern over three weeks, not at one bad day. The zones build on Kolding Talent's wellbeing model from Team Danmark's guide for parents: when a rider is in the yellow zone for a while, rider, parent and coach have a talk within 14 days, and in the red zone professionals are involved. The coach sees check-ins; the parents only if the rider shares them. Kadence never diagnoses.

reminders.title: Reminders
reminders.body: Kadence can remind you of the day's check-in in the evening, tell you when there is a new comment or the plan for the next days has changed, and give parents the week's overview on Sunday evening. Turn it on under Settings → Profile on the phone or computer you want them on, and choose which. On an iPhone it works once Kadence is on the home screen. The message itself from Apple, Google or Mozilla is empty; the phone asks Kadence what is new when it arrives. Between 21:30 and 7:00 reminders wait until morning. They are there when the installation has set them up.

devices.title: Uploads and devices
devices.body: Upload a FIT file from the bike computer, watch or trainer under Me, in the calendar or on the rider's page. Kadence reads the file itself, offline too, and puts the ride on the day's session when it fits. Every ride has its own page with curves, time in zones and best power. If Wahoo, Garmin or Polar is set up here, you can connect them under Settings → Devices, so rides come in by themselves. Wahoo and Garmin are US companies, Polar is Finnish, and it is the rider's own choice. Otherwise your rides come in as files, and that works just as well. A bike session can also be downloaded as .zwo, .erg, .mrc or .fit.

toDevice.title: Sessions on the bike computer
toDevice.body: A bike session with steps can go onto a Garmin, so you ride it with targets and a countdown on the screen. Plug the bike computer into the computer with a cable, press Send to bike computer on the session or Send the week's sessions on Me, and pick the bike computer when the browser asks. Kadence puts the files in the folder Garmin/NewFiles; eject the bike computer, and you find the sessions under Training. It works in Chrome and Edge on a computer and in Chrome on Android. In Safari and Firefox you download the files and put them in Garmin/NewFiles yourself. An Edge 540, 840, 1040 or 1050 does not show up as a drive on a Mac; use File Explorer on a Windows PC. Each session is named by its day first, such as 29.09 Tempo, so a week's sessions do not overwrite each other on the bike computer. A step without watts or pulse shows its target in words, such as RPE 7. Kadence writes nothing else to the bike computer and deletes nothing.

rulle.title: Rulle: the session on the trainer
rulle.body: When you can't get outside, ride today's session indoors in Rulle: in the menu, or "Ride indoors" on the session. Connect the trainer with one press. A smart trainer sets the watts of each block itself (ERG), so all you do is pedal; a trainer that only measures leaves the numbers to you. A heart-rate strap can be connected beside it. The screen shows the watts against the target, the time left of the block and the whole session as a bar you ride across, large enough to read from the bike. Space pauses, the right arrow skips to the next block, up and down make the session easier or harder. Stop pedalling, and Rulle pauses with you. When the session is over, the ride is saved as an ordinary ride on the session, and you say how hard it was. Without a connection the ride waits in the browser. Rulle needs Chrome or Edge on a computer or Android; on an iPhone, the Bluefy app can. With no session today, you can choose one of the team's own or DCU's standard sessions. M turns the sound off and on.
rulle.world: Now and then something small happens on the way – an electric cargo bike, a car with windscreen washer fluid, a dog – and pause long enough and you sit down at a café. They are counted in today's little things when you finish; the numbers and the bar are left in peace. Under the ride you hear the wind and the tyres with your speed, a bird in the country, a town's hum and the crowd on race day, so a hoot never comes out of silence. There are cheat codes hidden in Rulle. They cheat only the landscape, never the ride that is saved. You can choose between the routes – among them the championship lap from B&U DM 2026 in Vejle, with its finish at the top, the Future Racing lap through Copenhagen and the Worlds circuit round Mont-Royal in Montréal. K shows and hides the little map of the route. I hides every number, so you see only the rider and the land; tap the screen or press I again to bring them back. H shows the speed – the route's speed for your watts and a standard rider, so a guide, not a measure – and on a climb or a descent its percent is down in the corner. The rider on the screen stands on the steep climbs and gets low on the fast descents. The routes that come with Kadence run through the real land from OpenStreetMap – the woods, the lakes, the fjord and the towns – and you meet other riders on the road, some with a hand raised. The road crosses its rivers on bridges, and where you ride under a railway or a motorway, a train comes over now and then and the cars run on the bridge. On the city routes it is race day: a crowd down the finish straight and up the climbs, marshals with yellow flags at the islands and the sharp bends, marshals on motorbikes who hoot and ride a while ahead of you, cobbles that shake, speed bumps, a feed zone and the team buses. Copenhagen is a June morning in a big city – blocks in ochre, yellow and red brick, shops at street level, lamps hung over the street and a hot-dog wagon, Montréal a September afternoon with red maples, stairs outside the houses and the cross on Mont-Royal. The towns in the country, like Vejle, are built lower, in yellow and red brick under red and black tiles.

keys.title: Upload keys
keys.body: An upload key lets a program hand rides to Kadence by itself, without you being signed in. Create one under Settings → Devices → Advanced, give it a name, and copy it right away: it is shown that one time only. The program sends the ride's file to the address shown with the key, with the key in the Authorization field, written as Bearer and then the key. The ride lands on the day's session, exactly as when you upload it yourself. The key can only add rides for you. It cannot read anything, and you or your coach can remove it at any time. Give it only to the program that is to use it.

strava.title: From Strava to Kadence
strava.body: Kadence cannot be connected to Strava: Strava's rules for apps say an app may show your Strava rides to you alone, not to your coach. But you can bring your rides along. Your whole history: sign in on strava.com on a computer (the app cannot do it), choose Settings → My Account, press Get Started under Download your account and then Request download, and wait for Strava's e-mail; it can take a few hours. Put the zip file in the upload field under Me, as it is. Kadence shows what the archive holds, and then fetches the rides, or every activity if you choose so: with the names you gave them on Strava, newest first, and without the rides that are here already. Up to 500 rides a day; if there are more, it goes on where it stopped when you add the archive again the next day. If you have unpacked the archive, you can pick the folder with “Fetch from the device” instead. A coach can do the same on the rider's page. A single ride: open it on strava.com, choose ••• → Export Original, and upload the file. New rides come most easily straight from the bike computer; see Uploads and devices.

parentsPage.title: The child's page
parentsPage.body: A parent lands on their child's page, which the menu calls by the child's first name, or Your children with more than one. It shows the child's week with times and places, the next 30 days with the family's own days, the form in words and, if the child shares it, how things are going. The parents' guide is under Knowledge and help: Team Danmark's and Kolding Talent's ten themes and nine pieces of advice, written briefly in Kadence's own words with links to the originals.

ai.title: The AI
ai.body: The AI proposes, and the coach decides. It can read a coach's shorthand like "3x10 min Z4 / 5 min rest" into steps (the rules manage most of it without any language model), build a session from your own words with "Build with AI" in the library, compose a training programme in a conversation under Exercises and programmes, where every answer goes straight into the builder, propose a week under "Plan the week" for one rider or several, and write a short summary of the week's points of attention in the team's week. Nothing goes in the calendar until a coach presses. It never writes to a rider and never deletes anything. Week proposals and the summary read the riders' data, so they only work if the team has turned on "May the AI read the riders' data" under Settings → Team. Without a language model everything else works as before.

pilot.title: The first two weeks as a pilot team
pilot.body: If your team has just started out, there is a guide to the first two weeks: how to invite the whole team, lay out season plans for everyone, plan the first week and turn reminders on. It lives as docs/pilot.md in Kadence's code, and is the guide to the pilot team that Martin sends you.

thresholds.body: The zones are turned into watts and pulse from these.
thresholds.hint: Use the numbers from the latest test. Empty fields are fine: the sessions then show zones and feel.

explain.ftpWatts: The highest power you can hold for about an hour. The zones on the bike are worked out from it. You find it with a 20-minute test, where FTP is 95 % of the average, or by letting Kadence propose it from the rides.
explain.thresholdHr: Your pulse when you ride as hard as you can hold for about an hour. The heart-rate zones are worked out from it. It is typically your average pulse over the last 20 minutes of a hard 30-minute ride on your own.
explain.maxHr: The highest pulse your heart reaches. It is personal and says nothing about how good you are. You typically see it at the end of a hard sprint uphill, when you are warm.
explain.restingHr: Your pulse when you lie still in the morning, before you get up. It often falls as your form grows. If it is high some days, it can be tiredness or illness on the way.

pilot.title: The team's three numbers
pilot.body: Three numbers a week show how the team uses Kadence: how many riders check in, how many sessions get a receipt, and an estimate of the time spent planning. They are there to help decide what Kadence should be after the winter.
pilot.explainCheckins: Check-in: riders with a check-in on at least four days of the week.
pilot.explainReceipts: Receipt: sessions up to and including yesterday that are marked done, have an RPE or have a ride.
pilot.explainRiders: A rider counts from their first full week on the team. Archived riders do not count.
pilot.explainMinutes: Planning is a rough estimate in minutes, from when the coaches saved sessions, blocks and season plans. Changes less than ten minutes apart count as one sitting, and each sitting counts at least two minutes. Time spent thinking and reading the plan is not included. The number is there to help see whether Kadence saves time. It is not a judgement of anyone.

guide.title: The parents' guide
guide.body: Ten themes and nine pieces of advice on supporting a child who does a lot of sport, written briefly in Kadence's own words. Read the originals at Team Danmark.
guide.fromHelp: Ten themes and nine pieces of advice on supporting a child who does a lot of sport, sleep and school beside it, and what a parent can see here, and why.
guide.card: Ten themes and nine pieces of advice on supporting your child, sleep and school beside the sport, and what you can see here, and why.
guide.credit: Builds on Team Danmark's and Kolding Talent's guide for parents.
guide.guideLink: The parents' guide at Team Danmark

1.title: Why does your child do sport?
1.body: Talk about it, especially when something changes: a new team, an injury, a long spell without progress. If you each have your own reason, it easily causes friction later.

2.title: Before, during and after the race
2.body: Give calm before, be calm and kind during, and let your child talk to the coach and team first afterwards. Praise the effort whatever the result, and see to food and rest.

3.title: Working with the coach
3.body: Raise worries early and directly, at a good time. Let the coach coach, but keep an eye yourself on whether your child thrives in the environment.

4.title: Motivation
4.body: Rather ask "what did you learn today?" than "who won?". Wanting to get better lasts longer than wanting to win, also when things go against you.

5.title: Goals the child can control
5.body: Process goals, like keeping to the plan or practising a corner, are the foundation. Placings cannot be controlled. Do not share the results on social media.

6.title: You can get better
6.body: Mistakes and feedback are part of the way, not proof that you cannot. Your own way of talking about ability rubs off.

7.title: Feedback that helps
7.body: Compare your child with themselves, not with the others: young people develop at very different paces. Ask whether your child even wants feedback from you; they have a coach.

8.title: An everyday life that fits together
8.body: Make the week's plan together, with school, training, friends and time for nothing. At exams school comes first, at championships the sport. Sleep matters most.

9.title: Wellbeing
9.body: Hard spells are normal, but about three weeks of your child having a hard time should not just pass. Yellow means a talk within 14 days, red means help from professionals. Never train with pain or illness.

10.title: Boarding school and upper secondary
10.body: The transition is hard, and many stop here. Talk openly about the choices, and consider agreeing with the coach to cut back a little the first months.

1.title: You are a role model.
1.body: Your child sees how you behave at races, at training and in the club.

2.title: Support, but let your child stand on their own.
2.body: Help with the practical things, and hand over responsibility bit by bit.

3.title: Be a good part of the club.
3.body: Lend a hand, and respect the coach's work.

4.title: Keep an eye on wellbeing.
4.body: You are the one who can say no on your child's behalf.

5.title: Help the joy along.
5.body: The sport should be fun, in the long run too.

6.title: Find out what drives your child.
6.body: And make it broader than winning.

7.title: Praise the effort and what your child learns.

8.title: Remember everything else the sport gives.
8.body: Friends, belonging and things that are useful at school and in life.

9.title: Ask openly.
9.body: And compare your child with themselves, not with the others.

basics.sleepBody: Young people aged 14–17 need 8–10 hours of sleep. Fixed bedtimes, at weekends too, a cool, dark room and the screen away before bed help most. If your child is tired, check the sleep first.
basics.schoolBody: At exams school comes first, at championships the sport. Put school, exams and camps in the calendar, and the coach can take them into account. A session skipped to be with friends can well be a step in the right direction.

role.title: Your role as a coach of young riders
role.intro: The most important thing a coach of U17–U23 riders does is keep young people in the sport and help them develop. Results come after.

points.1: Development before results. A large Danish study of 7,110 young people aged 12–20 found that coaching focused on development, a say and belonging makes more of them continue the next season. A one-sided focus on results and controlling behaviour makes more of them stop, equally in elite and grassroots sport. The study did not include cycling, but the pattern held across the sports it covered.
points.2: Cycling is a sport of late entry. Physiology and body size matter a great deal, and late developers often catch up with those who were early. Do not judge talent on U17 results alone.
points.3: A healthy talent environment shows, among other things, in a suitable total load, patience, room for the whole person, psychological safety and support when things go wrong.
points.4: DIF's coach pledge puts it briefly: develop your athletes through good, fun and involving experiences, and start from each one of them.

safeguarding.title: Child certificates, boundaries and responsibility
safeguarding.intro: As a coach of young people you carry a special responsibility. The law sets the floor; sport sets a higher bar.

points.1: A child certificate (børneattest) is required by law for coaches with direct and ongoing contact with children under 15. A first-year U17 rider can be 14 until their birthday, so in practice it applies to every U17 coach. The club obtains the certificate.
points.2: DIF recommends a child certificate for everyone who coaches young people under 18, renewed every 2–3 years.
points.3: A sexual relationship with a person under 18 entrusted to you for teaching or upbringing is a crime (Danish Penal Code § 223). Agree in the club on what good physical contact is, and keep changing rooms separate.
points.4: Kadence is built for openness: there are no private messages between adults and young riders. Comments on sessions and rides are read by the coach, the rider and the rider's parents.
points.5: DCU runs courses for coaches: B&U Basistræner, Træner 1 and 2, and Kaptajn Landevej for safe group rides. On group rides, riders may ride two abreast where there is room and it causes no danger or undue inconvenience (Road Traffic Act § 49).

classes.title: The classes and the rules
classes.intro: DCU's classes go by birth year, and each class has its own race limits. Kadence works out the class for you.

points.1: U17 is the calendar year a rider turns 15 and 16, U19 17 and 18, and U23 19 to 22. The season runs from October to September.
points.2: U17 road races are at most {u17Road} km and time trials at most {u17Tt} km, and the gearing may be at most {u17Gear, number} m per pedal revolution.
points.3: U19 men race {u19mMin}–{u19mMax} km and U19 women {u19wMin}–{u19wMax} km, with time trials of at most {u19Tt} km. There is no gear limit in U19, since the UCI dropped the junior limit in 2023. Build up work on big gears gradually in the first year.
points.4: A stage race may last at most {youthStage, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} for U17 and U19 and {u23Stage, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} for U23. To enter the youth national championships, a rider must have ridden at least 3 licensed races.
points.5: The longest training ride is at most {u17LongH, plural, one {# hour} other {# hours}} or {u17LongKm} km for U17 and at most {u19LongH, plural, one {# hour} other {# hours}} or {u19LongKm} km for U19. The longest race is shorter than that, so there is no reason to train longer.

volume.title: Volume and season
volume.intro: Kadence plans from DCU's recommended hours for the rider's class and year and shows a corridor around them.

points.1: Stay close to the recommendations, both up and down. They are guidance for you as a coach.
points.2: In U17 the most important thing is to keep the volume moderate, so the motivation lasts. In U19 it is natural to raise the volume 10–15 % a year.
points.3: Avoid big jumps in volume, on training camps too. Build in lighter weeks, because recovery is often what releases the progress.
points.4: Do not stop completely in the winter. October is a break and free riding, and then the build starts again.

strength.title: Strength training
strength.intro: DCU's strength programmes, made by Team Danmark, are in Kadence's library with their progressions.

points.1: From November to mid-March, 2–3 strength sessions a week with at least 48 hours between them are recommended, then 1 a week. U17 and U19 riders should reach at least 30 sessions over the winter.
points.2: Strength training is not dangerous for young people and does not stunt growth. Give free-weight lifts time for technique before the load goes up.
points.3: Start with controlled repetitions with strength in reserve. DCU's own texts disagree on a few points, and Kadence shows the differences openly.
points.4: During the growth spurt, keep an extra eye on pain at the knee and the heel.

growth.title: Growth spurt and biological age
growth.intro: Two riders in the same year group can be years apart in development. That affects both what they can take and how their results should be read.

points.1: The growth spurt typically starts around 10½–11 for girls and 12½–13 for boys, but for boys anything from 10½ to 16. It lasts 2–2½ years.
points.2: The skeleton is not fully developed until around age 20, and some boys grow until they are 20–22.
points.3: Technique and coordination can wobble during the spurt. Turn down jumps in load, and take pain at the knee (Osgood-Schlatter) and heel (Sever) seriously.
points.4: A rider born late in the year can be almost a year younger than a teammate in the same class. Record height in Kadence and judge development alongside results.

injury.title: Pain, illness and concussion
injury.intro: Kadence shows points of attention, and the coach, the rider, the parents and in the end a doctor decide.

points.1: ATK's pain ladder is in Kadence's check-in. When pain changes the movement or stops training, the load comes down and a professional should look at it.
points.2: A fever means no training.
points.3: If concussion is suspected after a crash, the rider stops at once and sees a doctor. Danish guidance from 2024 allows light activity after 24–48 hours and a gradual return in six stages, where group rides and races come only when all symptoms are gone. The UCI requires juniors to wait at least two weeks after becoming symptom-free before racing again. The doctor decides.
points.4: On average it takes about 14 days to become symptom-free and 19 days to be fully back in sport. School comes back fully before full training.

sleepFood.title: Sleep, food and fluid
sleepFood.intro: Growing young people need more sleep and more food than one might think, and training only works when they get it.

points.1: Young people need 8–10 hours of sleep. Kadence's check-in shows sleep and warns when it is short again and again.
points.2: Regular meals and a snack before and after training. On rides over an hour, Team Danmark recommends 30–90 g of carbohydrate per hour.
points.3: Vitamin D, 10 µg a day from October to April. Girls need more iron after their first period, so with tiredness and frequent infections it is worth asking the doctor about iron.
points.4: Energy drinks with caffeine are not recommended for children and young people.
points.5: At camps and stage races with the same buffet every day, young people often eat less day by day. Keep an eye on it.

body.title: Body, weight and energy
body.intro: Cycling is a sport where talk about weight can do great harm. Kadence therefore has stricter defaults than most.

points.1: Team Danmark recommends, as a starting point, not weighing athletes under 18. Kadence goes further: no weight and no W/kg for riders under 19 unless the team turns it on.
points.2: Leave weight, body, food choices and portions alone, also as a joke, and talk about a rider's weight only in private. Every measurement needs a purpose and a conversation afterwards.
points.3: A Danish study from 2022 found signs of eating disorders in 23 % of female and 11 % of male elite athletes, and in even more at sub-elite level. Coaches' comments about weight loss were named as a trigger.
points.4: Signs of too little energy include a falling return from training, many injuries and infections, mood swings, and irregular or missing periods. The rider does not have to have lost weight. Refer to a doctor or sports dietitian, and do not calculate it yourself.
points.5: A missing period always goes to the doctor. Be open about the subject so riders dare to talk about it.

doping.title: Doping, medicine and supplements
doping.intro: The rider is always responsible for what they take, even when a supplement turns out to be contaminated. That makes good habits important early.

points.1: Strict liability means a positive test is the rider's responsibility, however the substance got into the body.
points.2: Under 18, ATK recommends no supplements other than vitamin D. Lists of performance supplements are written for adult elite athletes.
points.3: If supplements are used, only batch-tested products (for example Informed-Sport or the Cologne List), and keep the documentation.
points.4: Look medicine up with Anti Doping Danmark. Some asthma medicines are allowed up to a limit, while others, such as Bricanyl, need an exemption.
points.5: Since 10 February 2025 the UCI has banned CO-rebreathing equipment outside medical facilities.

wellbeing.title: Wellbeing and mental health
wellbeing.intro: Kadence's check-in helps you see how the riders are doing. It does not replace a conversation.

points.1: Team Danmark looks at mental health on four levels: the athlete, the training environment, the leadership and everyday life, each green, yellow or red. It is when someone stays in yellow or red for a long time that action is needed.
points.2: The parents' guide says: if a young person has struggled for about three weeks, have a talk within 14 days. Kadence shows when a rider has been in the yellow zone for too long.
points.3: In Team Danmark's 2024 wellbeing survey, 14 % had experienced boundary-crossing behaviour in the past year, most often belittling comments and comments about body and weight.
points.4: Help is available in the club, from DIF and from the municipality. For national-team environments, Team Danmark has EliteSupport.

school.title: School, exams and transitions
school.intro: Most U17 and U19 riders are in school, and school has to fit with the sport.

points.1: Put the school timetable and exams in the calendar. In exam periods, a lower load and lower expectations help.
points.2: The first months of a new upper-secondary school are hard. A couple of months with markedly less training can work wonders.
points.3: National-squad riders can apply for sporting approval for upper-secondary school with an extended programme and moved hand-ins and exams. The deadline is in January.
points.4: Agents make contact as early as U17 and U19. DCU offers independent advice on contracts.

heat.title: Heat and weather
heat.intro: Neither DCU nor Team Danmark has heat guidance for young riders. The advice here is Kadence's summary of general sources.

points.1: Sweat loss can reach 2 litres an hour. Drink steadily, but know that the body absorbs at most about 1–1.2 litres an hour. After the ride Team Danmark recommends 1.2–1.5 litres for every kilo lost.
points.2: Heavy sweating also costs salt, so think of salt on long, hot rides.
points.3: Move training to the morning or evening, and shorten the intervals on the hottest days.
points.4: The UCI's heat protocol for races judges the risk from both temperature and humidity.

parents.title: Working with the parents
parents.intro: Parents are the rider's most important support, and Kadence gives them a window in that the rider controls.

points.1: Parents see their child's training once the rider has confirmed the link, and check-ins only if the rider shares them.
points.2: The parents' guide from Team Danmark and Kolding Talent is under Knowledge and help in Kadence. Point parents there.
points.3: There is one open conversation: comments on sessions and rides are read by coach, rider and parents.
points.4: For riders under 18, DIF recommends thinking the parents into the plan.

classes.title: The classes and the way on
classes.intro: What the difference is between U15, U17, U19 and U23, what it costs, and how riders move on. For parents and riders who are new to the sport.

age.title: The class follows the calendar year
age.intro: A rider's class is set by the year in which the rider turns an age, and it stays the same all year.

points.1: U15 are those turning 13 and 14 this year. U17 turn 15 and 16, U19 turn 17 and 18, and U23 turn 19 to 22.
points.2: Each class spans two birth years, and U23 four. A rider is therefore always in the first or second year of the class. The class changes on 1 January.
points.3: A rider born late in the year can be almost a year younger than a classmate. It shows clearly in U15 and U17, where the body grows a lot.
points.4: In ordinary Danish races U23 riders race with the seniors: men in Herre A, B, C or D and women in Dame A or B, by points. U23 has a class of its own at the national championships and in UCI races.

distances.title: How far they race
distances.intro: DCU sets a longest distance for each class. It grows a lot from U17 to U19.

points.1: U15 race at most 45 km on the road and 15 km in a time trial.
points.2: U17 race at most {u17Road} km on the road and {u17Tt} km in a time trial.
points.3: U19 men race {u19mMin}–{u19mMax} km on the road, and U19 women {u19wMin}–{u19wMax} km. The time trial is up to {u19Tt} km.
points.4: In UCI junior races abroad a one-day race is at most 140 km for men and 100 km for women.

licence.title: Licence, trial tickets and what it costs
licence.intro: Licensed races need a licence from DCU. A rider can try it first.

points.1: The licence is free up to and including U15. From U17 it costs DKK 1,080 in Jutland and on Funen and DKK 1,215 on Zealand (2026). After 15 July the price is lower.
points.2: With a trial ticket a rider under U17 who belongs to a DCU club can ride three races without a licence for DKK 10 a race.
points.3: The rider needs their own liability and accident insurance. It is worth checking whether the family's insurance covers licensed races.
points.4: The entry fee is typically DKK 90–190, and a timing chip can be rented for DKK 50. Entering before the deadline is cheapest; a late entry often costs double.

raceDay.title: Race day: bike, radio and bottles
raceDay.intro: The young classes have their own rules for equipment and help on the way.

points.1: U11 to U17 race on an ordinary road bike. Time trial bikes, aero bars, disc wheels and wheels with fewer than 12 spokes are for the older classes.
points.2: The youth classes always race without radios.
points.3: Feeding during the race is allowed only in races over 100 km. A U17 rider therefore carries their bottles from the start.
points.4: Riders may give each other food, drink and tools on the way.
points.5: The youth championships for U11 to U17 require at least three finished licensed road races, and to ride the road race a rider must have started the time trial.

abroad.title: What opens up in U19 and U23
abroad.intro: From the year a rider turns 17, the UCI's international races open up.

points.1: U17 riders can ride national races abroad. The club reports the entry to DCU, and the country's own rules apply, gearing included.
points.2: Juniors in U19 ride the Nations Cup, the European and the World Championships for the national team. The Nations Cup decides how many riders Denmark may send to the Worlds.
points.3: U19 rides with free gearing. The limit went in 2023, when the UCI scrapped the junior limit.
points.4: U23 riders race with the seniors in Denmark and have races of their own on the UCI calendar, such as the Nations Cup and the Tour de l'Avenir.

teams.title: Teams, changing club and two dates
teams.intro: Many riders move from their club to a junior team when they reach U19. The rules give young riders peace until a sensible time to be approached.

points.1: U17 and younger ride for their club and in the club's kit. A DCU U19 team has four to nine U19 riders.
points.2: A team may approach a rider under 18 or the parents about next season from 15 June at the earliest. An agreement can be signed from 1 September of the year before at the earliest, by both rider and parent.
points.3: For a second-year U17 rider that means: approaches from 15 June, signing from 1 September, and the first race for the team when the season starts in U19.
points.4: DCU recommends a written agreement and a list of equipment showing what belongs to the rider and what is to be handed back.

nationalTeam.title: The national team and talent work
nationalTeam.intro: DCU runs a talent pathway over eight seasons: U17, U19 and U23.

points.1: In U17 there is a broad national squad of around 30 riders with winter camps. It is chosen on an assessment of potential and the points table, and during the season the performances in races count.
points.2: In U19 the squad is also around 30 riders. They send in their training and get feedback from the national coach. DCU sets no result targets for U19 and U23.
points.3: DCU describes talent as more than physique: the will to train, patience, and the ability to make sport, school and life fit together.
points.4: Young riders sign contracts earlier and earlier. DCU offers impartial guidance and says it rarely costs anything to wait a little with the big career moves.

school.title: School and sport
school.intro: There are schemes that make school and cycling easier to combine.

points.1: Team Danmark's schemes at upper secondary school require a place in DCU's national squad in U17, U19 or U23 and an individual assessment. They offer, for example, four years of upper secondary school and flexible absence for training.
points.2: From 2026 to 2029 a trial lets Team Danmark pupils take stx or hhx in three years with fewer subjects. 19 schools take part.
points.3: In years 7 to 9 many of Team Danmark's elite municipalities have sports classes with morning training, and several boarding schools have cycling on the timetable.
points.4: DCU itself mentions that longer schooling has a price too: a rider can lose their classmates and finishes a year later.

unwritten.title: The unwritten
unwritten.intro: How riders get onto a junior team is in no rulebook. Here is what the sport usually tells.

points.1: Junior teams typically look at results from U17, such as the youth championships, youth stage races and rounds of the U19 cup, and increasingly at power data. Attitude and the will to learn matter a lot too.
points.2: The big moves usually happen in two places: after the second year in U17, from club to junior team, and after the second year in U19, to a continental team, an elite team or a development team abroad.
points.3: The first offer is rarely the only one. Many riders break through late, and DCU's own message is that waiting a little can pay off.
points.4: It is a good idea to ask what being on the team costs: own contribution, equipment and travel. There are no public figures for it.

gearing.title: Gearing in the young classes
gearing.intro: Up to and including U17 the classes have a limit on how big the biggest gear may be.

points.1: The limit is {u17Gear, number} m per pedal turn in U17, {u15Gear, number} m in U15 and {u13Gear, number} m in U13 and U11. U19 and older ride with free gearing.
points.2: The tyre counts: a 28 mm tyre can take a bike over the limit that passes on 25 mm tyres. The gearing calculator works it out for your bike.

equipment.title: Equipment: where the speed is
equipment.intro: What buys the most speed for the money, and what is mostly for show. The figures are watts saved by a rider alone in the wind at 40 km/h, from wind tunnel and lab tests.
equipment.adults: Nearly all the measurements were made on adult riders, so for smaller riders the figures are an order of magnitude.

bunch.title: First: the bunch
bunch.intro: In a bunch riders shelter each other, and that puts everything else in perspective.

points.1: In the middle of a tight bunch a rider has only 5–10 % of the air resistance they would have alone. Second in a line has around 60 %.
points.2: In a road race a good place in the bunch therefore matters more than any piece of equipment, and it is something riders train.
points.3: Aero equipment matters most in time trials, breakaways and crosswinds. Rolling resistance and a clean chain matter as much in the bunch as alone.

free.title: The free and the cheap
free.intro: The first watts cost next to nothing.

points.1: A clean, lubricated chain: a chain left uncleaned after a ride in the rain costs around 6 W, and after a muddy ride around 12 W. Degreaser and lube cost DKK 100–300.
points.2: A lower, narrower position when the rider is in the wind saves 8–35 W. A bike fit can help, but practising the position matters most.
points.3: Clothes that fit close: an open, flapping vest cost 10 W in the wind tunnel. A race number pinned flat and tight follows the same logic.
points.4: Tyre pressure for the road: on a rough road the bike gets slower when the pressure is too high. How much that matters for a junior on Danish asphalt has not been measured.

tyres.title: Tyres and tubes
tyres.intro: This is where most is gained per krone, and the gain holds in the bunch too.

points.1: Fast race tyres instead of cheap training tyres save around 20 W for a pair at 40 km/h. A pair costs around DKK 800–950.
points.2: Latex tubes instead of ordinary butyl save 5–6 W for a pair and cost around DKK 200. They are almost as fast as tubeless, but lose air faster and need pumping before every ride.
points.3: Fast tyres often have a thinner tread. Many therefore train on sturdy tyres and race on fast ones.
points.4: Wider tyres are not automatically slower. Pumped to the same comfort, 23 to 32 mm roll almost the same.

kit.title: Clothing, helmet and overshoes
kit.intro: What flaps costs. What fits close is fast.

points.1: A skinsuit instead of a loose jersey and shorts saved around 10 W. Riders must race in the club's approved kit, so it takes a skinsuit in the club's design. Choose the right size; a suit that is too small works less well.
points.2: Aero overshoes saved around 6 W and cost DKK 420–480.
points.3: An aero road helmet saved 4.5 W on average against a vented helmet. When the helmet needs replacing anyway, the extra cost is small. The price says nothing about how well a helmet protects; independent helmet tests do.
points.4: The helmet must be CE approved with a chin strap, and it is replaced after a crash, even with no visible damage.

wheels.title: Wheels and bike
wheels.intro: The expensive equipment gives less per krone than many think.

points.1: Deep carbon wheels saved 4.6–6.6 W against shallow wheels and cost DKK 8,700–17,600. The test found almost no link between price and speed.
points.2: A new aero bike saved 17–32 W against a ten-year-old aluminium bike, wheels and bars included. It costs DKK 70,000–110,000.
points.3: A bike must weigh at least 6.8 kg. An extra kilo costs around 1.2 seconds per km on a 5 % climb, so weight matters less on Danish roads than many think.
points.4: From 2026 rims may be at most 65 mm deep in road races, and handlebars must be at least 40 cm wide. Wheels in road races must be UCI approved or traditional: a metal rim under 25 mm and at least 20 steel spokes.

cosmetic.title: What is mostly for show
cosmetic.intro: It is perfectly fine to buy something because it looks good or gives joy. It just does not make the rider faster.

points.1: A more expensive groupset, from Shimano 105 to Dura-Ace, is around 550 g lighter and costs around DKK 17,000 more. It brings no measured gain in watts; shifting is as precise at all three levels.
points.2: A ceramic bottom bracket saved 0.03 W against a good steel one.
points.3: Oversized pulley wheels save at least 2.4 W according to their maker. Nobody else has measured it.

training.title: Training tools
training.intro: A power meter does not make the bike faster. Its value is in the training.

points.1: Two small studies on adults found the same improvement whether intervals were set by heart rate or by power. A heart rate strap at DKK 356–699 is the cheapest start, and a chest strap measures more precisely than a watch.
points.2: A power meter makes sense when the coach uses watts to steer the training, and for learning to pace a time trial. A smart trainer already measures watts indoors.
points.3: Pedal power meters cost around DKK 2,400–5,500. Cheaper brands such as Magene also make power meters, heart rate straps and bike computers; we have seen no independent tests of their accuracy.

used.title: Buying used
used.intro: Growing riders often change bikes, and used can be a good buy.

points.1: Choose the frame size for the rider's measurements now, not one to grow into. Seat post and stem can adjust a little; a frame that is too big never gets smaller.
points.2: Signs of a crash: new bar tape or new cables on an otherwise older bike, scuffs on bars, levers and saddle, and a bent derailleur hanger.
points.3: Carbon can be tested by tapping lightly with a coin along the tubes: sound carbon gives a clear note, damaged carbon a dead one. If the bike has crashed, have a carbon workshop look at it before buying.
points.4: A repaired carbon part no longer counts as UCI approved without the maker's consent. Check too that wheels and bars meet the rules, and that the gearing can be kept within the limit.

value.title: Most speed per krone
value.intro: Watts saved by a rider alone at 40 km/h. 10 W is around 17 seconds in a 15 km time trial. The gains cannot simply be added together.

food.title: Food and drink for young riders
food.intro: What young riders need day to day and on race day, how to make the energy yourself, and how to look after their teeth. For parents and riders.

everyday.title: Everyday food
everyday.intro: Growing riders need energy enough for training, school and growing. Ordinary food covers most of it.

points.1: Team Danmark recommends 5–7 g of carbohydrate per kg of body weight a day with less than 1½ hours of training, and 7–10 g per kg with more.
points.2: On days with hard training over 1½ hours, half the plate can be carbohydrate, a quarter protein and a quarter vegetables. On lighter days the Danish Food Administration's Y plate fits: 2/5 carbohydrate, 1/5 protein and 2/5 vegetables.
points.3: Growing teenagers are advised 1.2–2.0 g of protein per kg a day. Most get it from ordinary food, spread over the day's meals.
points.4: Breakfast before morning training helps. If eating early is hard, a small portion and a sports drink during the session can do it.

timing.title: Before, during and after
timing.intro: When the food is eaten matters almost as much as what.

points.1: A main meal 3–4 hours before training or racing, or a snack 1–2 hours before with easy carbohydrate, a little protein, little fat and little fibre.
points.2: Under 45 minutes, water is enough. From 1 to 2½ hours, 30–60 g of carbohydrate an hour is advised, and on long races up to 90 g once the gut is used to it. The energy calculator works it out for a race.
points.3: Straight after: 1–1.2 g of carbohydrate per kg and 10–20 g of protein, and a main meal within 1–2 hours.
points.4: Ordinary food can easily give 50 g of carbohydrate: two bananas, two slices of bread, 2.5 dl of cooked rice or 1 dl of raisins.

fluid.title: Fluid and salt
fluid.intro: In Danish weather riders typically sweat 0.7–1.2 litres an hour, and more in the heat.

points.1: For training over an hour or in the heat: at least 1–2 dl every quarter of an hour, and 2–3 dl with heavy sweating. The body can take up around 1–1.5 litres an hour.
points.2: Weight lost in sweat should be at most 2 % of body weight below 25 °C and 1 % above 30 °C. A rider can weigh before and after a session and then knows their sweat rate.
points.3: For hard training over an hour, 500–700 mg of sodium per litre helps. Urine should be pale yellow and clear.
points.4: Drink no more than you sweat. A rider who gains weight during a session has drunk too much, and a lot of fluid with too little salt can be dangerous.

homemade.title: Homemade energy
homemade.intro: Sports drink, rice cakes and bars can be made at home for a fraction of the price.

points.1: Ordinary sugar is already half glucose and half fructose, a mix the body takes up well on long races. Two parts sugar to one part glucose gives the ratio 2:1.
points.2: Sports drink should have 4–8 % carbohydrate (40–80 g per litre) and 500–700 mg of sodium per litre. In the heat fluid matters most, so use the weaker bottle and eat the rest.
points.3: For comparison, a bought gel with 25 g of carbohydrate costs DKK 25–30, and a homemade rice cake with 32 g DKK 0.40–1.40.

safety.title: Keeping it safe in a jersey pocket
safety.intro: In a jersey pocket food is close to body temperature, so homemade food is treated as fresh food.

points.1: Cooked rice can form toxins if it cools slowly. The Danish Food Administration advises cooling from 56 to 10 °C within four hours, so cool rice cakes quickly in small portions.
points.2: Make rice cakes the evening before, keep them in the fridge, and take them straight from there. Eat them within the first couple of hours of the ride, and in the heat within the first hour. That is Kadence's suggestion from the USDA's rule of thumb.
points.3: Baked oat bars are dry and keep better at room temperature. Store them airtight and eat them within a few days.
points.4: Mix sports drink on the day, and rinse and dry the bottle after use.

teeth.title: Teeth
teeth.intro: Sugar many times a day, acid and a dry mouth during training make riders prone to cavities and erosion.

points.1: Among the athletes at the London 2012 Olympics, 55 % had cavities and 45 % erosion, although most brushed twice a day.
points.2: Rinse the mouth with water after gels and sports drink, and drink in bigger gulps rather than many small sips.
points.3: Brush with fluoride toothpaste (1450 ppm) morning and evening, and spit without rinsing, so the fluoride works longer. High-fluoride toothpaste (5000 ppm) needs a prescription and is given from age 16.
points.4: Tell the dentist that the rider trains a lot and uses sports products. Municipal dental care in Denmark is free until the age of 22.
points.5: Sugar for training is needed to perform. See dental care as a way of managing the risk, and drink water day to day.

supplements.title: Supplements and caffeine
supplements.intro: Ordinary, varied food covers what young riders need.

points.1: Anti Doping Danmark writes that the vast majority of children and young people have no need for supplements.
points.2: Supplements can contain substances on the doping list that are not on the label. Among popular supplements the risk of a contaminated product is 10–15 %, and close to 50 % for tablets (Team Danmark). The rider is always responsible.
points.3: If supplements are used anyway, choose products tested by, for example, Informed-Sport or the Kölner Liste, and keep the batch number and the receipt.
points.4: Caffeine: for those under 18 the limit is 3 mg per kg of body weight a day and at a time, with cola, coffee and caffeinated gels added together. For a 55 kg rider that is 165 mg.

lowEnergy.title: When the energy falls short
lowEnergy.intro: When the body gets too little energy for its training, it is called relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs). It affects girls and boys alike, and it mostly happens without anyone meaning it to.

points.1: It typically arises when training grows, when school and cycling both need fitting in, when appetite goes after hard sessions, or when the rider does not get to eat on long rides.
points.2: It rarely shows on the scales, because the body lowers its metabolism. Signs in both sexes: growth slows, training gives less, the rider is often tired, ill or injured, has mood swings or sleeps badly. A resting heart rate under 50 can be a sign in young people.
points.3: In girls, periods can stop or become irregular. In boys, sex drive can drop and morning erections become fewer.
points.4: Talk about energy, recovery and being able to keep training, and leave weight and body shape out of it. Say what you have noticed, and suggest a talk with a sports dietitian or a doctor.
points.5: See a doctor straight away for fainting or dizziness when the rider stands up.

drink.title: Everyday bottle, about 6 % (1 litre)
drink.method: Stir the sugar and salt into the water, and pour in the juice.
drink.carbs: 58–60 g of carbohydrate and 590 mg of sodium per litre. A 750 ml bottle gives 43–45 g of carbohydrate.
drink.price: DKK 4–7 per litre. With 60 g of sugar and a little lemon instead of juice it costs around DKK 0.50.

fuel.title: Fuel bottle, about 8 % (750 ml)
fuel.method: Stir everything into a little lukewarm water, and top up with cold. For races over 2½ hours.
fuel.carbs: 60 g of carbohydrate (8 %) at a ratio of about 2:1 and 470 mg of sodium. With 60 g of sugar alone the ratio is 1:1.
fuel.price: DKK 1–2.50 per bottle, against DKK 15–20 for the same carbohydrate from bought powder.

riceCakes.title: Sweet rice cakes (10 pieces)
riceCakes.method: Cook the rice under a lid until soft and the water is absorbed, stirring often. Stir in the sugar, dates, salt and spice while the rice is warm. Press it into a 20 × 20 cm dish lined with baking paper, cool quickly, and cut into 10 pieces. Wrap each in baking paper or foil.
riceCakes.price: Around DKK 1.35 per piece. Without dates and with 120 g of sugar in all, DKK 0.42.

oatBars.title: Baked oat bars (8 bars)
oatBars.method: Melt the butter and honey, and fold in the oats, dates and salt. Press into a 20 × 20 cm tin lined with baking paper, and bake at 175 °C for 20–25 minutes until golden. Cut into 8 bars while warm.
oatBars.carbs: 32–34 g of carbohydrate per bar. The bars have fat and fibre, so they suit long, easy rides and before the start best.
oatBars.price: DKK 3–4 per bar, against DKK 17–22 for a bought energy bar.

measure.title: How the commissaire measures

steps.1: The bike is put in its biggest gear: biggest chainring and smallest sprocket.
steps.2: One pedal is set straight down over a mark on the floor.
steps.3: The bike is rolled slowly backwards, so the rear wheel turns the cranks.
steps.4: When the pedal has turned once, the distance is measured. It must be within the limit.

measure.note: This is how it is done in practice in several countries; DCU's rules do not go into the method in detail. In a time trial the gear check must be done at least 10 minutes before the start.

results.intro: General advice from Team Danmark and DCU for the day you chose. The amounts fit a typical rider in the class, so take a little more or less by hunger and experience.

goal.carbsOne: around {high} g of carbohydrate an hour

dayBefore.title: Fill the stores
dayBefore.drink: Drink steadily all day, at least 1½ litres and preferably water. Your urine should be pale yellow and clear.
dayBefore.eat: Eat plenty of carbohydrate at the day's meals, such as pasta, rice, potatoes, bread and oats. Then the stores in your muscles are full when you start.
dayBefore.dcu: DCU suggests a short ride to open the legs the day before a race: about 1 hour with 5 minutes at threshold (AT) or 3 minutes all out.

dinners.pasta: Pasta with meat sauce and salad

before.early: With a start at {start} the main meal falls before 6 o'clock. If you are not up that early, eat a smaller breakfast as soon as you are up, a light snack before the start and sports drink on the way.
before.title: Before the start
before.mealNote: Eat more or less of it to land around the goal. Go easy on fat and lots of fibre, so the stomach is ready for the start.
before.snackNote: Keep the snack light, so it does not sit in the stomach. Drink a little at a time in the hours before the start.
before.snackNoteTraining: If you train in the morning, have breakfast first. If that is hard just before training, eat a little and drink sports drink on the way.

during.how: Drink a little at a time, 1–2 dl every quarter of an hour, and eat a little about every half hour. Start in the first hour, before you get hungry or thirsty.
during.recipe: You can make sports drink yourself: 8 dl water, 2 dl orange juice, 40 g sugar and ¼ tsp salt make 1 litre with about 6 % sugar. Salted water is the same without the juice and sugar. The bottles in the example are {ml} ml.

budget.title: Why can't you eat it all back on the way?
budget.body: A race in a bunch uses
budget.stomachKcal: around {g} g of carbohydrate = {kcal} kcal an hour
budget.note: Even with a full stomach, carbohydrate covers only around {most} % of what the body uses in an hour. The body takes the rest from its stores in the muscles and liver. That is why the day before and the meal before the start count so much.

after.goal: For {rider} within the first half hour:

after.soon: The next 4 hours: {low}–{high} g of carbohydrate every hour
after.hard: You ride hard again tomorrow. Eat plenty of carbohydrate for the rest of the day, and drink steadily, so the stores are full by tomorrow.
